messages.subject: How to get started
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Sorry, I know these questions are on the dumb side, but I'm having trouble getting oriented. Where can I go to get an overview of JRI, REngine, and possibly others? 

In the rJava distribution, I see 3 jar files in the jri directory but no documentation (the javadoc section with the package is for rJava). There are two examples (btw, the run.bat script does not work under Windows); while examples are helpful, they do not substitute for an explanation.

I can find documentation online at http://www.rosuda.org/R/nightly/JavaDoc/, but nothing that gives an overview. There are classes org.rosuda.JRI.Rengine and org.rosuda.REngine.REngine that seem similar, but are not the same. There are two classes named REXP also. The stuff in the REngine side of things is essentially devoid of documentation - we mostly just have the class names and methods; while the JRI classes are better documented but seem to be older. 

So what is the distinction between the JRI classes and the REngine classes, and how do I know which to use? FWIW, what I want to do is start Java from R (at least usually), and have my Java code call R code as well manipulate variables within an R environment. I have an initial try that works, using JRI classes/methods, but it seems like the code I'd need to evaluate or assign within an environment would require a lot of parsing and hence be inefficient.

Finally, I'd also appreciate more overview-type documentation of the rJava package. While each R function is documented, it is very difficult to know which of the hundreds of functions we want to know about first. Again, the website has examples, but not an overview. 

Sorry for the nuisance questions, but any guidance will be appreciated.

Russ

In the beginning there was org.rosuda.JRI. It contains the low-level API (rni* = R Native Interface) and a slightly higher level (e.g., parse/eval). It was specific for JRI only it a little ad-hoc and you may benefit from the knowledge of R internals to use it.

Over time there was a demand to unify the Rserve and JRI interfaces since they both offer a large common set of functionality - interface from Java to R. The result is

org.rosuda.REngine

That is the modern, recommended API to use with both JRI and Rserve. It is designed to be backend-agnostic and it much cleaner to work with (in JRI you had to check return values, with REngine there is exception handling instead). The documentation consist essentially of the JavaDoc.


> So what is the distinction between the JRI classes and the REngine classes, and how do I know which to use? FWIW, what I want to do is start Java from R (at least usually), and have my Java code call R code as well manipulate variables within an R environment. I have an initial try that works, using JRI classes/methods, but it seems like the code I'd need to evaluate or assign within an environment would require a lot of parsing and hence be inefficient.
> 
> Finally, I'd also appreciate more overview-type documentation of the rJava package. While each R function is documented, it is very difficult to know which of the hundreds of functions we want to know about first. Again, the website has examples, but not an overview. 
> 

There are really very few functions in rJava for "regular" use. For the high-level API there is just J() - that's all. For the low-level API there are two main functions .jnew and .jcall with a few that it is useful to know but quite self-explanatory like .jcast and .jarray/.jevalArray - that's pretty much all for most users... But what doI know, I wrote the package ;) That's why it would take someone else to write some kind of introduction or so ...

Cheers,
Simon

> library(rJava)
> .jinit()
> .jengine(TRUE)


This only creates org.rosuda.JRI.Rengine - the low-level part. However, down below, you're using the high-level REngine class, so you want to do something like:

e <- .jengine(TRUE)
je <- .jnew("org/rosuda/REngine/JRI/JRIEngine", e)

Depending on your setup, you'll need to add the corresponding REngine and JRIEngine classes, in recent rJava it's something like

.jaddClassPath(system.file("jri",c("REngine.jar","JRIEngine.jar"),package="rJava"))


A small word of warning - starting Java this way (R -> Java -> loop back) is not recommended, because on many platforms system libraries differ for threaded and non-threaded programs, and since R is not threaded, it will use single-thread libraries. However, Java requires multi-thread libraries, so the only reliable way is to start Java first and then start R (see JGR).

Cheers,
Simon

The run.bat script that comes with the latest rJava (0.9-2) does not work (nor do earlier ones I have seen). Here is its contents on my system:

	set PATH=%PATH%;C:/PROGRA~1/r/R-213~1.0\bin;C:/PROGRA~1/r/R-213~1.0\lib
	C:/JDK1~1.6-I/bin/java -cp .;examples;JRI.jar;src/JRI.jar rtest $*

In fact, there are several obvious reasons that it can't possibly work. Here are the defects I can identify. It may not be exhaustive.

	- Forward slashes instead of back-slashes in DOS paths
	- C:/JDK1~1.6-I does not exist on my system
	- The argument 'rtest' should not be there (should be provided by the user on the command line)
	- The argument '$*' is for unix, not Windows
	- A path to jri.dll is needed
	- The script keeps adding redundant stuff to the PATH if run repeatedly
	   (this won't keep it from working, but is a defect nonetheless)

I do not have administrator rights to my PC, so have another directory in my R_LIBS path to install R packages. When I install rJava there, it creates a different run.bat script:

	set PATH=%PATH%;d:/Rcompile/recent/R-213~1.1\bin;d:/Rcompile/recent/R-213~1.1\lib
	C:/Progra~2/Java/JDK16~2.0_1/bin/java -cp .;examples;JRI.jar;src/JRI.jar rtest $*

Russ,

First the main take-away points:
- it seems you did not install rJava from sources, so the run.bat script is was not created for your machine to start with
- there is a bug in the generation of the run script: it doesn't take into account multi-arch R installations, simply \bin has to be replaced by \bin\i386 for multi-arch R


Now to the long story:

On Jul 20, 2011, at 5:09 PM, Lenth, Russell V wrote:

> The run.bat script that comes with the latest rJava (0.9-2) does not work (nor do earlier ones I have seen). Here is its contents on my system:
> 
> 	set PATH=%PATH%;C:/PROGRA~1/r/R-213~1.0\bin;C:/PROGRA~1/r/R-213~1.0\lib
> 	C:/JDK1~1.6-I/bin/java -cp .;examples;JRI.jar;src/JRI.jar rtest $*
> 
> In fact, there are several obvious reasons that it can't possibly work.

In fact none of those points is a reason for the script to fail (if installed on the machine), but we'll address them one by one.


> Here are the defects I can identify. It may not be exhaustive.
> 

It is not, it does miss the only issue why the run script may fail for some installations (or in fact only for very recent R versions), but let's get to your list first:


> 	- Forward slashes instead of back-slashes in DOS paths

Forward and backward slashes are equivalent in Windows - they were not in DOS - but that was a long time ago ;)


> 	- C:/JDK1~1.6-I does not exist on my system

That name is a 8.3 (short) path name as generated by Windows. Again, this is equivalent to the full name and is used in Windows to avoid quoting issues. You can see short filenames using dir /X - e.g.

C:\>dir /X

 Volume Serial Number is 7079-5DC3

 Directory of C:\

10/18/2010  10:55 AM    <DIR>          JDK1~1.6-X   jdk1.6-x64
06/25/2010  02:14 PM    <DIR>          PROGRA~1     Program Files
07/15/2011  11:45 AM    <DIR>          PROGRA~2     Program Files (x86)
01/21/2010  05:38 PM    <DIR>                       Users
06/07/2011  04:09 PM    <DIR>                       Windows
               0 File(s)              0 bytes
              17 Dir(s)   1,526,804,480 bytes free

At this point I suspect that the installed rJava is a binary from RForge.net, because it would have to be a coincidence to name your Java installations the same way I did (the above dir output is from the RForge.net Windows VM).


> 	- The argument 'rtest' should not be there (should be provided by the user on the command line)

The purpose of this file is to run the rtest class, so, obviously, it has to be there.


> 	- The argument '$*' is for unix, not Windows

Fair point, although irrelevant to the function since rtest doesn't actually take any arguments


> 	- A path to jri.dll is needed

No, it's not, because the current directory is automatically included in the java library path.


> 	- The script keeps adding redundant stuff to the PATH if run repeatedly
> 	   (this won't keep it from working, but is a defect nonetheless)
> 

I'm not sure what you are referring to - the environment in batch files is local, so it is added only once.
 

> I do not have administrator rights to my PC, so have another directory in my R_LIBS path to install R packages. When I install rJava there, it creates a different run.bat script:
> 
> 	set PATH=%PATH%;d:/Rcompile/recent/R-213~1.1\bin;d:/Rcompile/recent/R-213~1.1\lib
> 	C:/Progra~2/Java/JDK16~2.0_1/bin/java -cp .;examples;JRI.jar;src/JRI.jar rtest $*
> 
> It has the same mix of forward and back-slashes, incorrect arguments, etc.; but this time I do get a correct path to Java.

Again, you did not configure JRI for your machine, this time you took the CRAN binary and Uwe likely uses the default target for Java installation. The indication of a CRAN binary is 'd:/Rcompile' since Uwe uses his own build of R as opposed to CRAN releases.


> On the other hand, the directory 'd:/Rcompile/recent/R-213~1.1' does not exist on my system.
> 

I presume you used rJava binary from CRAN -- that obviously won't reflect your settings, because the settings are detected at compile time. R does not provide a way for packages to update their configuration when installed from binaries -- binaries are simply unpacked from the zip file. Therefore you would have to install the packages from sources to reflect your settings. The more realistic scenario is to edit the file to match your needs.


> It seems likely to me that the script has never been tested in Windows;

It has been tested and it did work. It still does work for singe-architecture R. Now we come to the actual issue -- R has changed Windows binaries recently by installing multiple architectures in parallel so it can work both in 32-bit and 64-bit. This has changed the paths to R.dll, so the only modification of the run.bat script you have to turn \bin into \i386\bin if you use multi-arch R. That is the only issue I can see and it can be addressed in JRI.


> and that, in general, the Windows installation scripts for this package do not work correctly and do not make use of the R_LIBS environment variable.


There is no "installation script" and I suspect you did not even run any. Also R_LIBS is entirely irrelevant in this case, as none of the settings involve the paths inside rJava. If you want a more comprehensive example, have a look at the JGR launcher - that illustrates how to set PATH properly and pass on the proper parameters to Java in order to select the architecture you want to use and to allow operation from any directory.


> (Slightly off-topic but related is that the JGR software and package also do not make use of R_LIBS and also cannot find Java.)
> 

Given the results so far I'm not convinced. JGR provides ways to specify custom library locations - in fact you only have to do it once because it is recorded in the preferences. However, it is not something I use, so I'm not ruling out the presence of bugs - but we'd need more details. Analogously, lack of the ability to find Java is likely due to the lack of the proper Java installation - you'll have to match the Java installed (32-bit vs 64-bit) with R and JGR (both 32-bit and 64-bit are supported but all Java+R+JGR launcher have to be of the same architecture). That said, I'd like to encourage you to supply the details so in case there is an issue, we can address it. The stress is on details and facts, though.

Thanks,
Simon

Starting a new thread on this part of my previous posting...

Here's what I did and what happened. Numbers refer to chronological order.

1. In R, I used
       install.packages("JGR")
Since I have an R_LIBS environment variable, the package was installed in my own directory rather than the library directory in the R installation tree.

2. I downloaded jgr-1_62-x64.exe from the R-Forge website.

3. I Attempted to install the above. I got a message that it would to install the JGR package (which I had just installed). So it was not paying attention to R_LIBS, and it should. At that point, installation failed because I do not have administrator access.

4. I got our computer-support guy to run the JGR installer as administrator. This time, as might be predicted from the previous step, it installed the JGR package in the C:\program files\R\R-2.13.1\library, even though the package was already installed in my directory.

There are two separate settings: R_LIBS is the list of library paths for R and then there is --libpath argument to JGR which defines the library to be used for the installation of JGR. So if you want to use other than the system library location, you should set R_LIBS to contain your custom location and then run jgr --libpath=my/library, e.g.:

set R_LIBS=c:/users/urbanek/Rlib

Originally, those were intended as independent settings - so you can have custom R_LIBS yet have the launcher install JGR in the system location. Note also that R_LIBS will be stored in the preferences so it only needs to be set once and saved as a preference. That is the intended use.
In retrospect it would be probably useful to infer --libpath from R_LIBS if not set, but that was not the original intention - mainly because it was not expected that Windows users will modify environment variables on a regular basis (note that due to the bootstrap sequence you can't use .Rprofile or .Renviron).

But that is your responsibility. The reason for the existence of jri.ignore.ule is that it is static code so you can't catch the exceptions, but if you instantiate Rengine it's your responsibility to catch the exception and/or check that jri is loaded. The default is to abort so if you set jri.ignore.ule you are assuming responsibility from there on.

Cheers,
Simon
